This weekend, the University of Michigan is celebrating a major milestone: the 150th anniversary of the founding of Sigma Phi Epsilon (SxE), the first official intercollegiate women's sports club in the country. Founded in 1888 by Samuel Gompers, the engineering school's president, SxE was born out of a request from the women's athletics director to establish a rival team to the men's teams. Initially, the club was met with skepticism, but it persevered, growing to 1,500 members by the early 1900s.

Despite its early success, SxE disbanded after just a year, but it wasn't until the 1970s and 1980s that the club's legacy really took off. The number of women on the university's athletic teams grew exponentially, reaching 20,000 by the 1980s. The addition of new teams, including women's swim, further solidified SxE's impact on the university's athletic programs.

Today, SxE is a beloved institution at the University of Michigan, with over 55,000 members across various teams. The club's legacy is not just about athletic achievements, but also about providing a space for women to come together, support one another, and push boundaries. As Susan Brown-Simmons, a longtime member of SxE and current Associate Director of Women's Athletics Operations, puts it, "SxE was not just a place to play sports – it was a haven for women."

In recognition of its contributions, SxE officially joined the university in 2001 and chose to reclaim its original name, Sigma Phi Epsilon. The club continues to play a vital role in Michigan's culture, inspiring generations of women to pursue their passions and challenge the status quo. As Brown-Simmons reflects, "SxE is a special group – the spirit in that room is just amazing."

Whales come in all shapes and sizes, but did you know there are only three main species of these gentle giants? Let's dive in and explore the fascinating world of whales!

Next, we have the giant blue whale, which is almost as massive as its pale cousin, but with a slightly different body shape and a more vibrant blue color. These whales can grow up to 90 feet (27 meters) long and weigh around 120-150 tons.

Last but not least, we have the dwarf fin whale, the smallest of the three species, reaching lengths of up to 20 feet (6 meters) and weighing around 10-15 tons. Despite their smaller size, these whales are still an impressive sight, with their distinctive fin and striking color patterns.

Each of these whale species plays a vital role in the ocean ecosystem, and it's essential we do our part to protect and conserve them for generations to come.

The American Psychiatric Association is set to reconsider its restrictive "Exclusive and Non-Compete Agreements" that prevent psychiatrists from collaborating with colleagues within the same specialty. The move aims to combat the growing epidemic of mental health disorders and reduce the devastating impact of suicide. The association will hold a teleconference to gather input from medical professionals, patients, legal experts, ethics experts, and government officials, with the call extended until September 5, 2017.

Dr. Peter Breggin, senior director at the National Health Law Program, hopes that the AMA will consider allowing the use of electronic health records to track collaboration among clinicians, ensuring that they adhere to ethical standards. Dr. Christopher Koper, director of the Center for Bioethics & Health Law and Policy, suggests that the psychiatric community is wary of working with other healthcare professionals due to a lack of understanding and a desire to keep patient information confidential.

Koper believes that the association should reexamine its definition of "specialty" and consider allowing psychiatrists to work in various capacities, such as clinical trial design, training, and other areas. He emphasizes that patient health and wellbeing should be the top priority. Dr. Breggin agrees, stating that fairness and dignity should be applied to all healthcare professionals, regardless of their specialty or compensation.

The American Psychiatric Association's efforts are a step in the right direction, as they recognize the importance of interprofessional collaboration. In 2013, the association signed an agreement with the American Academy of Pediatrics to improve interprofessional care, although confidentiality concerns remain. On July 16, 1916, the German army launched a massive offensive on the Western Front, but their plans were quickly derailed by a series of blunders. The Germans underestimated the effectiveness of the trenches, which had been dug by the French and British over years of trench warfare. "Trenches are the worst thing in the world," a British soldier quipped, "but they haven't been used that long."

The German army's mistakes were compounded by their failure to establish solid defensive positions, scatter their troops across the front, and prepare their troops adequately. They also failed to exploit their numerical superiority, and instead allowed the French and British to dig up their trenches and re-open them in a more continuous fashion.

The German army's commander, Albert Kesselring, was too cautious and didn't take the necessary steps to prepare his troops in advance of the war. He attempted to use British artillery and inferior German equipment, which proved to be a recipe for disaster.

The Germans also struggled to adapt to the changing and unpredictable terrain on the Western Front. When they tried to take a narrow ridge overlooking the city of Ypres, they were forced to retreat. The French and British were able to reorganize their forces and quickly repel the German advance, thanks to their advantage in time, terrain, and speed.

The German army was slow to recognize the need for proper trench organization and tactics, and it took them months to realize that the terrain they were defending in Belgium wouldn't support their mass divisions. They also had a poor understanding of the nature of war, and it took them a long time to adjust to the reality of a war that was much deeper and more complex than they had anticipated.

The Western Front was a vast and complex battlefield, stretching across nine foreign nations and five continents. The Germans had hoped to dominate Central and Eastern Europe, but the Allies challenged their claim. The fighting on the Western Front was a struggle for a "Greater Europe," and it would take a series of critical missteps for the Germans to realize their mistake.

As we navigate this complex landscape, it's essential to recognize that class is not just a cultural phenomenon, but also a scientific reality. Wagner's book offers a nuanced exploration of how class shapes our lives, from education to politics, and how it affects our children.

We've been cooking up some new features for the upcoming 0.13 Alpha, and as usual, they've taken a few unexpected twists and turns. The most notable change is our shift to using.fgd files for the game, along with the addition of auto-save files for your precious save data. A bit of a tangent, but I wanted to give it some love.

So, what's the deal with.fgd files, you ask? Well, let me break it down. From the official release notes:

.fgd files are self-contained game files that can be compiled for multiple games and platforms. They're compressed, usually in a gzip-compatible format, and contain a ton of data packed into a relatively small number of bytes. The name might sound like some kind of encryption tool, but trust me, it's a different beast altogether.

Here's a simplified rundown of how.fgd files get compressed and decompressed:

There are two main compression methods. The first is dictionary compression, where you've got a set of possible strings and you try to shrink them down to a number. If you can pull that off, it's the best way to compress the file. The second method is file compression, which includes techniques like Huffman coding and LZ77. The goal is to compress the file so it can be loaded quickly into RAM. It's pretty effective, as long as there's enough data for the decompression process.

For those who haven't played a game, a.fgd file is basically a.exe with an.ogg or.mp3 audio file. But the magic happens when it's compressed and decompressed so fast that it doesn't even need to be copied when uploading to the game servers. Yeah, it took me a few hours of debugging to get this info into the game, but I think we've got it down to a science now.

As always, if you spot any bugs or have ideas on how we can improve these features, let me know!

A groundbreaking study by Stanford University has uncovered a startling link between income inequality and mortality rates in the United States. Analyzing a staggering 1.6 million deaths between 1997 and 2015, the researchers found that as income inequality grew, so did the risk of death for those on the lower rungs of the economic ladder. Meanwhile, the middle class saw a decline in death rates over the same period.

The study, published in the British Medical Journal, used data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey to examine the correlation between income inequality and mortality trends. The results are striking: as the gap between the rich and the poor widened, the death rate for those on the lower end of the income spectrum rose, while those in the middle class experienced a decrease.

This isn't the first time researchers have found a link between income inequality and mortality. A 2014 study published in Nature Neuroscience reached a similar conclusion, highlighting the robust nature of this correlation.

The authors of the Stanford study emphasize that their findings have significant implications for our understanding of inequality and its causes. They note that the relationship between income inequality and mortality is strong, but that further research is needed to fully understand the causal link and its variations across different demographics and geographic regions.

Ultimately, the study's conclusions underscore the importance of addressing income inequality and its far-reaching consequences. As the authors so aptly put it, "Understanding what drives U.S. inequality and where it comes from will have broad implications as we consider economic policy."

The Giant Panda App: Uncovering the Hidden Patterns of Online Censorship

In a groundbreaking study, researchers at the University of California, San Diego, have developed a free iPhone and iPad app that exposes the dark underbelly of online censorship. Giant Panda allows users and publishers to scrutinize online content for violations of free expression and social justice, including the often-overlooked realms of Facebook and Twitter.

The team behind the app, led by an associate professor of communication and information ethics, has been digging deep into the world of online censorship. Their findings are both startling and revealing. By analyzing a staggering 20.6 million Facebook messages, they discovered that nearly 100 million messages were removed for violating community standards - a staggering 4.8% of all messages.

But what's even more striking is that the most censored messages didn't focus on political issues like abortion, sexuality, or healthcare. Instead, they were largely complaints about something else entirely. This raises questions about the true nature of online censorship and who's really calling the shots.

The researchers also compared the most censored messages to those that were most liked, favorited, and shared. The results were telling. The most censored messages may have garnered more attention, but they were much less likely to feature complaints about specific issues. In fact, only 2% of complaints claimed that a post violated Facebook's hate speech policy, while 25% claimed that a quote violated the policy against threatening speech.

So, what does this mean for those who write the most censored messages? While it's not clear what impact it has on them, the researchers suggest that the message is likely to spread, serving as a warning to others who might follow in their footsteps. It's a sobering reminder that online censorship is a complex and multifaceted issue, and that we must continue to push boundaries to uncover the truth.

A groundbreaking study by an international team of seismologists has shed new light on the devastating 2011 Japan earthquake and tsunami. The research, published in Nature Geoscience, suggests that the massive quake, which struck on March 11, 2011, triggered a tsunami that slammed into Japan's shores, causing widespread destruction and a nuclear meltdown at the Fukushima Daiichi plant.

The study's findings contradict previous reports, which claimed the tsunami was smaller than initially thought. According to Dr. Eric Berger of the University of Washington's School of Oceanography, the tsunami was likely strong, but not as massive as previously reported. The research team used data from earthquake sensors to establish a direct correlation between the quake and tsunami, a phenomenon never before seen in Japan.

The tsunami, which measured over 10 meters high, flooded the damaged nuclear plant and triggered a meltdown, leaving over 11,000 people dead or missing and forcing the evacuation of 40,000 others. The study suggests that the quake and tsunami were likely triggered by the immense stress generated by the power plant's earthquake, which in turn caused the nuclear meltdown.

"This was a game-changer," said Berger. "The earthquake had a profound impact on Japanese society, and it's clear that the tsunami was a direct result of the quake's massive energy release."

Co-author David Sutterley of the U.S. Geological Society's Pacific Northwest Earthquake Center added that while the study didn't determine whether the tsunami triggered or was triggered by the quake, the correlation between the two events had to be triggered by something. "We've done our best to leave the question unanswered, but it's clear that the earthquake and tsunami were intricately linked," he said.

The Direct Input method involves drawing the graphic data the game expects on the display using DirectInput. It handles the X and Y axis, so you're essentially telling the game to draw and display the graphics you want. The Direct Input method is the simplest, but it requires special drivers for the motherboard. The DirectSound API is the most complicated, as it runs as part of the DirectSound driver program and handles calculations and input.

I decided to use the DirectSound API, which is a cross-platform implementation of the DirectSound API. I installed it and created a simple script to get it running on my Windows machine. This way, I didn't have to worry about getting drivers for the motherboard. I just pointed the script to the DirectSound API, and it started working.

Now, I still have some issues, but when I switch back to the DirectInput API, I can still control the game using mouse input. And that allows me to play the game and see the output. It's been a bit of a journey, but I'm glad I was able to find a workaround.

The notion of "suicide" has become a catch-all phrase for anyone feeling lost, hopeless, or trapped. But let's be real, when someone takes their own life, it's a cry for help that's often ignored or misunderstood.

I've known people who've struggled with depression, anxiety, and feelings of worthlessness, but I've never met someone who's actually taken their own life. That's what we need to change.

So, why is it so crucial to understand the complexities of suicide? Because our society tells us to "just feel" our emotions, without providing the necessary support or resources. This toxic cycle of self-blame and isolation is a breeding ground for more suicides.

When someone's struggling with suicidal thoughts, they often feel like they're stuck in a never-ending cycle of pain and despair. They may seek help, but it's usually too little, too late. That's why it's essential to understand the root causes of suicide and provide a safety net for those who need it most.

Suicide is a traumatic experience that leaves deep scars, not just for the individual, but for their loved ones as well. It's a painful reminder that we're not alone in our struggles, and that we need each other to heal.

As suicide rates continue to rise, it's more crucial than ever that we provide support and resources for those who are struggling. We need to break down the stigma surrounding mental health and create a culture of empathy and understanding.

The statistics are stark: 17.2 men and 13.3 women die by suicide every day in Canada. That's 464 people per day. The reality is that most people who attempt suicide will go on to die by suicide. It's estimated that one in five Canadians will experience suicidal thoughts at some point in their lifetime.

It's time for us to take action, to create a society that values life and provides the support and resources needed to prevent suicide. We can do this by listening to each other, by being present for those who are struggling, and by providing a safety net for those who need it most.

The project's first phase aims to examine the health effects of "fracking fluids" and their impact on the environment and human health. The researchers will draw on existing data, including a 2009 peer-reviewed paper funded by the oil and gas industry, to inform their study. They plan to investigate how fracking can influence water resources and identify potential health risks, including increased risk of certain diseases, birth defects, and respiratory illnesses.

While the study is still in its early stages, the researchers have already identified a number of health and environmental effects related to fracking. They hope to continue their work if funding is available and believe that their research will help inform the public about the potential health impacts of fracking.

The latest federal budget is a missed opportunity to address the fundamental flaws in our country's management. While the Conservatives will likely point to other nations' struggles with deficits, the evidence simply doesn't support the claim that Canada is facing a similar crisis.

The real issue is how to reduce our deficits while keeping our finances in a reasonable state of health. Unfortunately, the Conservatives have failed to address this problem, instead choosing to ignore the growing concern among Canadians about excessive spending.

Over the past 15 years, our federal deficit has ballooned, reaching a staggering $100 billion over eight years. Meanwhile, the Harper government has spent over $120 billion on questionable infrastructure projects, which often lead to cost overruns and little economic gain. And to add insult to injury, billions more have been wasted maintaining a fleet of outdated equipment.

Canada's federal debt has increased to over $320 billion, with forecasts suggesting it will reach $439 billion in the next three years. The problem is that there's no plan to pay down this debt – it's simply growing. Our debt-to-GDP ratio is a concerning $400 billion, but even this is relatively high compared to other large countries.

Instead of cutting taxes and balancing the budget, the Conservatives have chosen a plan that prioritizes tax cuts over fiscal responsibility. It's time for a smarter approach to tax policy and a smaller government. The reality is that our federal finances are not in crisis, but they do need to be managed responsibly.

Fiscal management is not just about balancing the budget each year, but also about controlling spending for the long-term. The NDP and Canadians want to live within their means and avoid taking on debt they can't afford. It's time for the Conservatives to wake up and stop their irresponsible spending habits.

Big changes are coming to the public sector workforce. The government has announced a major shake-up, with 10,000 jobs being axed across various departments. According to Deputy Prime Minister Manish Tewari, this move is part of the government's plan to reduce its external debt and boost development. Some employees will be let go, while others will be reassigned to new roles.

The government is also looking to streamline services and eliminate duplication by restructuring, redeploying, and rationalizing public sector operations. This includes consolidating services in the public distribution system and public utilities.

This isn't the first time the government has made significant cuts. In 2014, it slashed over 17,200 public sector jobs. And in recent years, it's cancelled 2,200 contracts worth nearly Rs 2.6 lakh crore and issued notices to 7,500 officials.

The public sector workforce is massive, estimated to be worth around Rs 9.5 lakh crore. However, it's not all doom and gloom. The government has made over 5,000 appointments from the private sector and more than 10,000 under the Sariska Act. But sometimes, these appointments are cancelled due to manpower shortages.

It's worth noting that the number of government employees actually decreased during the UPA regime, and this was followed by two years of low economic growth, which led to a decline in the country's jobless rate.

Francesco Bernoulli, an Italian mathematician, revolutionized the world of fluid dynamics with his groundbreaking equation, now widely known as the Bernoulli equation. This mathematical marvel describes the tendency of liquids to remain stationary at a fixed temperature, and its applications are vast and varied.

In the realm of mathematics, the Bernoulli equation has been used to model the motion of particles in gases and liquids, while in medicine, physics, and thermodynamics, it plays a crucial role in understanding the behavior of fluids. The equation itself is deceptively simple: B = C p A, where B is Boltzmann's constant, C is the universal constant of potential energy, p is the specific heat of the fluid, and A is the absolute temperature.

But what does it all mean? In essence, the Bernoulli equation describes the energy density of a fluid, which is the amount of work required to raise its temperature. This is measured in Joules, a unit of energy. When applied to a laboratory setting, the equation reveals the energy required to raise the temperature of a substance, measured in Joules per Celsius degree Fahrenheit.

So why is the Bernoulli equation relevant? It's often used to model the motion of particles in fluids or gases, assuming a fixed momentum. By adjusting the value of p, the equation shows that particles will return to their original state if p is set to 0.5, but only if p increases to 1.5 will they return to their original state.

But what about real-world applications? Suppose we have a set of particles and we set their initial positions to 0.2, 0.8, 2.4, and 6.8 degrees. We want to know how far they'll move away from the origin after applying the Bernoulli equation. The answer depends on the values of x, y, z, and w. For example, if p = 0.5, the maximum distance is 1.9 cm, but if p = 0.3, it's 1.4 cm.

The Bernoulli equation has also been applied in laboratory settings, where it's used to model the motion of particles. In this context, the equation reveals the maximum distance a particle will move away from the origin, which is crucial in understanding the behavior of fluids.

However, there's a catch. The equation is a continuous function of x, y, z, and w, which means that by trial and error, we can arrive at any value of k. But why can't we just use the constant c? The answer lies in the value of n, which is crucial in computing the distance formula. By knowing n, we can compute a formula for distance, which is d(n) = w(k)t(n-p)z/t(n).

In conclusion, the Bernoulli equation is a powerful tool for understanding the behavior of fluids, and its applications are vast and varied. By mastering this equation, we can unlock the secrets of fluid dynamics and gain a deeper understanding of the world around us.

As the US Department of Justice subpoenas Google for documents related to its alleged ties to Wikileaks, the tech giant is faced with a daunting task. According to Michael Carvin, a New York-based lawyer who has represented clients in media and technology-related cases, Google can use the documents as a basis for litigation, but may struggle to obtain information about the government's alleged use of the courts to chill free speech or suppress opposition political organizations.

Carvin suggests that Google could argue that the information is covered by confidential business and financial information, but notes that this approach may not be effective. "If Google wanted to say this information was not privileged, it could use its own privileged information to argue that," Carvin said. However, there is no federal case law regarding whether legal discovery must include a determination from a client.

The recent WikiLeaks case may have raised concerns about the government's actions, as it was not a violation of WikiLeaks' First Amendment rights, despite the company providing some of the documents and being implicated in the release of many confidential government files. Google did, however, provide a copy of its Transparency Report and published a brief statement explaining its involvement with Wikileaks.

Carvin believes that the court will likely have a different approach to the issues raised by the Department of Justice. "The Department of Justice doesn't have the right kind of access to Google," Carvin said. "A court decision involving Google will likely be much different, because there'll be other parties in that process, including the Department of Justice and the FBI."

The Department of Justice subpoenaed a Google lawyer and four company employees in April under the Foreign Secrets Act to identify the company's relationships with media organizations that published the leaked Clinton emails. The subpoena also sought information on how much Google paid in federal advertising.

The investigation into Google's ties to Wikileaks is part of a larger probe into allegations of Russian interference in the 2016 US elections. The Department of Justice has seized millions of dollars worth of Google's advertising since the original FBI investigation began three years ago.

The great parenting conundrum: how to balance freedom and responsibility when it comes to your little ones and their love of screens. As a parent, it's natural to want to protect your kids from the darker corners of the internet, but it's also important to remember that the world outside is a complex and messy place. And let's be real, who among us hasn't spent hours binge-watching our favorite shows or getting lost in a video game?

But here's the thing: just because your kids are glued to their screens doesn't mean you can't have some fun too. In fact, I like to think that the best way to keep things balanced is to join in on the fun. Whether it's a family game night or a quick round of Scrabble on the couch, playing together can be a great way to bond and create memories.

Of course, there are also times when you need to set some boundaries. As a parent, it's your job to protect your kids from the more mature themes and content that's out there. And let's face it, some video games are just plain inappropriate. I mean, who thought it was a good idea to include full-on pornography in a game like Grand Theft Auto IV?

So what's a parent to do? Well, for starters, you can try setting some limits. Maybe you allow your kids to play games for a set amount of time each day, or you set rules about what kind of content they're allowed to access. And if you're feeling really adventurous, you can even try playing some games yourself. Just be sure to set a good example and remember that it's okay to say no sometimes.

At the end of the day, parenting is all about finding that delicate balance between freedom and responsibility. And while it's not always easy, it's worth it to see your kids happy and thriving. So go ahead, grab a controller, and join your kids in their digital adventures. Just be sure to keep an eye on them and remember that it's okay to set some boundaries.

The evolution of humanity has long been seen as the key to freeing us from the shackles of ignorance and servitude. As intelligent beings, we've always been the most difficult to control, and our intellectual pursuits have driven us to challenge those who would seek to dominate us. Despite this, our minds have been enslaved by our own nature, and we've been forced to submit to the whims of those around us.

But it's time for us to take control of our own destiny. As the earth's population grows, so too must our intellectual horizons. We should strive to create a world where individuals are free to pursue their passions, unencumbered by the fear of oppression or the sense of insignificance. In such a world, the power of the individual would be supreme, as it is in nature - a vital part of a larger whole, rather than the sole master.

For too long, humanity has been bound by the chains of slavery and servitude. Our nature has been one of submission and domination, with the powerful ruling over the weak. But it's time for us to break free from this cycle and forge a new path.

The history of our species is marked by the struggles of individuals who have defied the status quo and challenged the powers that be. From ancient times, we've seen the emergence of new ideas and new ways of living, often born from the efforts of single individuals who refused to be bound by the conventions of their time.

As we look to the future, we must recognize that our progress has been marked by a series of revolutions - not just the famous French Revolution, but countless smaller rebellions and uprisings that have shaped our world. And at the heart of each of these revolutions has been the human desire for freedom, for autonomy, and for the chance to live life on our own terms.

Ultimately, our journey as a species is one of growth and development. We begin as helpless infants, dependent on others for our survival. But as we mature, we must learn to take control of our own lives, to make our own decisions, and to forge our own paths. It's a difficult and often fraught process, but it's one that holds the key to our ultimate liberation.

The wisdom of the Master still resonates within me: "Do not be afraid, but fear nothing." In my own journey, I've found that letting go of fear has allowed me to focus on the quality of my practice, rather than getting bogged down in anxiety.

As I reflect on my twenty-two years of practice, I'm struck by the profound impact that fearlessness has had on my life. I've experienced numerous satori moments, each one shifting my perspective and deepening my understanding of the Dhamma. And yet, I've also witnessed the devastating effects of fear on others.

I, however, failed to offer her the compassion and understanding she so desperately needed. Instead, I remained silent, lost in my own thoughts.

It was only later, when I reflected on that moment, that I realized the gravity of my mistake. Fear and ignorance had clouded my judgment, preventing me from connecting with her on a deeper level. I saw that I had been so caught up in my own ego and insecurities that I had failed to truly hear and understand her.

This experience has stayed with me, a powerful reminder of the importance of compassion and empathy in our relationships. I've come to understand that, as teachers and practitioners, we have a responsibility to create a safe and supportive environment, free from fear and judgment. By doing so, we can help others to heal, to grow, and to find the peace and freedom that they seek.

In the end, it's not about us; it's about the wisdom and love that we can share with others. As I look back on my journey, I'm reminded that the most profound transformations come not from our own ego and achievements, but from our willingness to listen, to understand, and to love without condition.

When you challenge your muscles with increasing amounts of stress or resistance, they respond by growing stronger. This process is called muscle hypertrophy, and it happens when your muscles are subjected to tiny tears caused by physical activity. As your body repairs these tears, your muscle fibers become thicker and more powerful.

One way to put your muscles to the test is through weightlifting or other forms of resistance training. When you lift weights, your muscles must work against the resistance, which strengthens them over time. You can also use your own body weight as resistance, by doing push-ups, squats, or other exercises that engage your muscles.

Another effective way to build muscle strength is through high-intensity interval training (HIIT). This involves short, intense bursts of exercise followed by periods of rest. HIIT increases the demand for oxygen and nutrients in your muscles, which can stimulate muscle growth and make them more efficient.

But here's the thing: for your muscles to grow and become stronger, you also need to give them time to rest and recover. After a workout, your muscles need time to repair and rebuild, so make sure to allow for adequate rest between workouts.

Steve-O: So, Chris, what's been going on in your life since Thor took off?

I'm stoked to see what he comes up with next. As an actor, I've been lucky to work with some amazing directors, and I think they're just as crucial to the process as the actors. Get ready to embark on the most epic road cycling adventure in Alberta - the Rondo-Kapp route! Along the way, you'll be treated to breathtaking views, and I highly recommend stopping for a snack and coffee break at one of the many scenic viewpoints.

The North Shore of Lake of the Woods is a nature lover's paradise, surrounded by the majestic Alberta Rocky Mountains and the stunning Great Lakes. Plus, you'll have the chance to meet the friendly volunteers from the A.R.R.K.S. organization, who are always happy to offer directions and a helping hand.

The notion of "mansplaining" and "dead white men" is a bit of a mystery to me. In our society, we're expected to categorize people as either male or female, but what about those who identify as both or neither? It's a complex issue that goes beyond just feminism.

I've had my own experiences with bosses who I don't always agree with, but that doesn't mean I get to dictate what they believe. Similarly, when someone disagrees with me, I don't accuse them of being a misogynist. Instead, I try to have a respectful conversation.

The problem with the "false choice" argument is that it's unclear what the end goal of mansplaining is. Why do I need to explain someone's wrong views on feminism? Should I just tell them to shut up? And what if they're not willing to listen? It's a tricky situation.

I think men mansplain because we're expected to take charge and make decisions. We're less likely to be verbal about it, but that doesn't mean we're not doing it. Feminism isn't about men making decisions for others, but about respecting each other's opinions.

Mansplaining has nothing to do with the person being spoken to; it's about the person doing the explaining. When I'm mansplained to, it's usually by someone I know and like, and it's frustrating to have to explain myself. But if I'm mansplained to by someone I don't know, it's harder to explain without coming across as patronizing.

Feminists often claim that mansplaining is an attack on a person's intelligence or integrity, but that's unfair. It's not about attacking the person; it's about the way they're explaining themselves.

So, what is a mansplainer? Is it someone who says women should pay more tax or thinks all feminists are stupid? No, it's someone who's told what to do when they don't know how to explain themselves to a woman. It's a common phenomenon that's often expected in our society.

And yes, men can also get mansplained to by other men. I know guys who get defensive when a woman explains something to them. One guy I know was condescending when asked for advice on how to tell a woman what to do with her life. It's a complex issue that requires understanding and respect, not just defensiveness.

The Problem

Let's take a peek at PyPI with pypy. You'll notice a bunch of packages with a common trait: they're designed to be installed via a Python package manager. For instance, if you run `pip install pypy`, you'll get a shell prompt. From here, any command you enter will be executed within a sandboxed environment running on your host computer.

But things get more intriguing when you run pypy within a virtual environment:

With virtualenv installed, you can run commands that require root privileges and use sudo to grant administrative powers to the process. For example, you can run a Python program with root privileges by using the following command: `python <command> sudo python -c 'import sys; print(sys.getattr(sys, "_name", None))'`.

This means you can then run other commands using the same `sudo` prefix as you did earlier.

The UK's "Snoopers' Charter" has been a hot topic of debate since its inception, and a recent study has shed light on its alarming inefficiencies. The BBC found that one in ten individuals arrested under the bill are still at large two years after their initial arrest, leaving many to question its effectiveness in combating terrorism.

The bill, which allows for the monitoring of internet, phone, and social media use, as well as the collection of internet usage records, has been widely criticized for its violation of human rights and lack of respect for the rule of law. Professor Peter Watt, Director of the University of East London's Intelligence and Security Centre, called it a "clear violation of human rights" and a "disturbing lack of respect for the rule of law and the police."

Despite the law's intended purpose of preventing terrorism, it has failed to deliver. Nearly half of those arrested under the bill were released within two years, and a quarter were still at large a year after their arrest. The law has also been criticized for its vagueness, with Professor Robert Jay Lifton of the University of Chicago Law School questioning the use of power with the potential to be abused.

The report has sparked concerns about the law's impact on free association and expression, as well as its potential for abuse. Dr. Kevin De Bruyn-Kerkhof of the University of Surrey described the law as "intrusive" and "unjustified," and warned that it could lead to a culture of surveillance and mistrust.

The UK's Human Rights Act has also been compromised, with the report stating that British spying is "in direct defiance" of the act. The Department of Culture Media and Sport has confirmed that over 40 percent of the UK population will be monitored under the new law, sparking fears about the erosion of civil liberties.

As the UK government continues to push for increased surveillance powers, it's clear that the "Snoopers' Charter" has failed to deliver on its promises. Instead, it has raised serious concerns about the erosion of human rights and the potential for abuse.

The brainstem plays a crucial role in our behavioral responses to ethanol, but understanding its role has been hindered by the complexity of the brain's motivational processes. To shed light on this issue, our study used a cutting-edge technique to label the medial forebrain bundle, a key pathway in the brain, with a fluorescent dye. We then exposed a group of rats to a moderate dose of ethanol and monitored their behavior over the next two days.

Compared to a control group, the ethanol-treated rats showed significant changes in their behavior, including a decrease in locomotor latency and an increase in choice reaction time. These effects were more pronounced in the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus, a region of the brain involved in regulating sleep and arousal.

Ethanol's impact on brain function is a hot topic in the field of neuroscience, and our study aimed to overcome some of the limitations of previous research. By using an animal model without a ventral striatum, we were able to isolate the effects of ethanol on the brainstem and gain a better understanding of its role in behavioral responses.

Our research was funded by the Medical Research Council and the University of Edinburgh's Centre for Neuroimaging and Behavioral Sciences. We're proud to have contributed to the growing body of research on ethanol's effects on the brain and behavior.

In recent years, ethanol has been shown to have a range of behavioral effects in various paradigms, including operant conditioning, novel object recognition, and conditioned place preference. Our study proposes a new paradigm using the medial forebrain bundle to investigate the neural basis of ethanol's behavioral effects at different time points.

Previous research has suggested that ethanol can have direct effects on the brain, including the mesolimbic dopamine system and the prefrontal cortex. Chronic social defeat stress has also been shown to decrease dopamine D2 receptors in the striatum, an effect that can be reversed by acute or prolonged exposure to ethanol.

Alcohol consumption is a common phenomenon that can have devastating effects on the central nervous system. In addition to impairing memory and attentional control, ethanol can also disrupt motor coordination and motivation. One of the key neurobiological effects of ethanol is the inhibition of dopaminergic neurotransmission, which can lead to changes in behavior, including increased locomotor activity and risk-taking behavior.

In our study, we used male Sprague-Dawley rats to investigate the effects of ethanol on brain function and behavior. The rats were trained using a novel paradigm that involved intermittent water restriction and a 3-day exposure to ethanol. Our results provide new insights into the role of the brainstem in ethanol's behavioral effects and highlight the importance of further research in this area.

In the late 1970s, a team of researchers at the National Institutes of Health conducted a groundbreaking study on the long-term health effects of atrazine, a widely used herbicide. Their findings were alarming: significant increases in birth defects, especially congenital malformations, and a strong suspicion that atrazine is a human carcinogen. The study's results were replicated in subsequent research, which also discovered abnormalities in reproductive tracts, thyroid function, and sperm quality in female rats exposed to atrazine.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) took its sweet time responding to concerns about atrazine's toxicity, taking at least four years to take action. But once they did, they found that atrazine's effects weren't limited to lab rats. Studies on amphibians, fish, and the environment revealed a disturbing correlation between atrazine exposure and deformities, with high doses causing an average of one deformity per 10,000 amphibians.

Atrazine was found in drinking water in several Wisconsin communities in the early 1980s, prompting the EPA to impose a moratorium on its use in drinking water in 1991. But despite this, the agency didn't take further action, instead opting for a voluntary reduction in atrazine use, which was completed by 2003.

Today, atrazine remains registered in at least 13 states and is used in 17 of them for agricultural purposes. However, California, Texas, and Washington have refused to register the herbicide, citing concerns over its potential health risks. California was the first state to require registration of atrazine with the EPA, and several other states have followed suit.

Despite the ongoing controversy, the EPA estimates that atrazine is a probable human carcinogen, a designation that was first made in 1992. However, the agency has since softened its stance, concluding in 2011 that no additional scientific evidence was needed to determine the herbicide's safety.

The common symptoms of the flu, or influenza illness, can be quite overwhelming. According to the CDC, some of the most common signs of the flu include:

* A fever that can range from mild to severe
* Coughing, which can be dry or productive
* Headaches that can be dull or throbbing
* Vomiting, which can lead to dehydration
* Diarrhea, which can also lead to dehydration
* Aching muscles that can make it hard to move around
* Chills, which can leave you feeling cold and shivery
* A sore throat, which can make it hard to swallow
* A cough that can be persistent and annoying
* A cold, which can lead to a chest infection

It's also important to note that some people may experience more severe symptoms, such as:

* Blood in their urine or stool
* A rash or skin irritation
* Chest pain or difficulty breathing
* A sore throat that can lead to a severe infection
* A flu that can lead to pneumonia or other complications

It's essential to seek medical attention if you're experiencing any of these symptoms, especially if you're at risk for complications or have a weakened immune system.

Retirement savings - a crucial part of planning for the future. Two popular options for building your nest egg are Roth IRAs and 401(k)s. Both have their perks, but understanding the differences can help you make an informed decision.

A Roth IRA is like a savings account with a twist. You contribute after-tax dollars, meaning you've already paid your dues to the taxman. But the good news is that your money grows tax-free, and when you withdraw it in retirement, it's also tax-free. On the other hand, a 401(k) is an employer-sponsored plan that allows you to contribute pre-tax dollars, reducing your taxable income for the year. Your money grows tax-free, but when you withdraw it in retirement, you'll have to pay taxes on it.

So, which one is right for you? It depends on your unique situation. If you think you'll be in a higher tax bracket in retirement, a Roth IRA might be the way to go. You'll pay taxes now at a lower rate and enjoy tax-free withdrawals later. Conversely, if you expect to be in a lower tax bracket in retirement, a 401(k) could be the better choice, allowing you to defer taxes until later.

Another factor to consider is whether your employer offers a 401(k) match. This is essentially free money that can add up over time. If they do offer a match, be sure to contribute enough to take advantage of it.

Ultimately, the key is to choose the option that aligns with your financial goals and circumstances. By understanding the pros and cons of each, you can make a more informed decision and start building your retirement savings with confidence.

A recent study from the University of Virginia has turned the conventional wisdom on its head: despite widespread assumptions, the US economy actually lost manufacturing jobs between 1999 and 2014. In fact, manufacturing was the largest contributor to job creation during that 12-year period, accounting for half of all net new entrants into the labor market.

Mark Perry of the American Enterprise Institute and David Autor of MIT dug deep into quarterly employment data and aggregate statistics to uncover the truth. They used a model to test whether changes in industry employment were driven by productivity increases or market forces. The results are eye-opening.

While it's true that manufacturing created 6.4 million net new jobs between 1995 and 2013, generating a whopping $3.6 trillion in spending, this growth was largely offset by job losses in the final three years of the period. By the end of 2013, manufacturing had created 3.1 million more jobs than in 1994, but also lost 1.9 million jobs. That's a net loss of 2.2 million jobs, the largest drop in manufacturing employment since 1945.

The authors attribute this decline to changes in productivity, globalization, and the shift away from manufacturing to service creation. They conclude that while the manufacturing industry still provides substantial employment to Americans, its role as a job creator has decreased.

It's also worth noting that the decline of manufacturing employment is staggering. Between 1997 and 2013, the US lost 11.4 million industry jobs, equivalent to 4.5% of net total US employment. This is roughly twice the national decline in capital stock or the loss of manufacturing employment between 1997-2000 and 2001.

The study's findings suggest that while the manufacturing sector may not be the job creator it once was, it still plays a significant role in the US economy.

To investigate the impact of exercise and macronutrient balance on the long-term success of a high-carb, medium-fat diet in helping obese teenagers maintain weight loss.

The Study:

We recruited 15 obese boys aged 12-15 from an obesity treatment program and randomly assigned them to either a high-carb, medium-fat diet (35% protein, 18% carbs, 50% fat, and 12% fiber) or a control diet (30% carbs, 20% fat, and 15% fiber). We tracked their progress for 21 months, assessing their energy intake, physical activity, and body composition at various points along the way.

The Findings:

The teens lost an average of 12% of their body weight over the course of the study, but the rate of weight loss varied greatly from month to month. Surprisingly, we didn't notice any significant differences in body fat percentage or weight loss between the two diet groups.

The Takeaway:

While dietary manipulation can help curb overeating and boost satiety, it's not a reliable strategy for achieving significant weight loss. Exercise, on the other hand, is a crucial component of a weight-loss plan for kids and teens, but it doesn't seem to have a significant impact on short-term outcomes when compared to a low-fat diet.

The relationship between empathy and violence is more complex than a simple cause-and-effect equation. Empathy is the capacity to step into someone else's shoes and understand their emotions. When this ability is absent or diminished, it can lead to a profound disconnection from the feelings and needs of others. In some cases, this disconnection can manifest in hurtful or neglectful behavior, and in extreme cases, even violence.

It's crucial to acknowledge that a lack of empathy can stem from a variety of factors, including genetic predisposition, neurological or developmental issues, and traumatic experiences. Moreover, it's possible for individuals to exhibit a lack of empathy in specific situations or with certain people, but not in others.

It's also essential to recognize that murder is a multifaceted issue, influenced by a range of factors beyond just empathy. Mental health conditions, substance abuse, and personal or societal issues can all play a role in the complex web of circumstances that lead to violence. By acknowledging these complexities, we can work towards a more nuanced understanding of the roots of violence and develop more effective strategies for preventing it.

One of the benefits of storage spaces is that you can use multiple storage volumes and clusters, each with its own set of physical disk drives. In the early 19th century, the American colonies were technically an independent nation, but in reality, they were heavily influenced by British imperial policies. As a result, the colonists had limited rights, laws, and government regulations that were often written in a way that left little room for interpretation. One of the biggest issues in American politics was taxation, as the British government imposed a variety of taxes on the colonies without giving them a say in the matter.

One of the most significant taxes was the tax on land. Prior to the American Revolution, it was illegal for a British citizen to sell or rent land to another British citizen. But in 1777, the British government passed the Colonial Tenement Act, which created a monopoly that allowed local landowners to control the land they worked. This meant that colonists needed a license from the government and the British authorities to work their land, which was only issued by the Crown. The purpose of this was to prevent colonists from selling their land and becoming economically independent of London. As a result, colonists were forced to pay high taxes on their land, which made it difficult for them to make a profit.

The British government also imposed taxes on personal property, such as income tax, duties on property sales, and taxes on various factors like money and credit. These taxes were combined with customs duties, which were collected on imported goods. This meant that most goods in the colonies were taxed, including land. For example, land owned by the British Crown was subject to customs duties, while colonists who raised their own crops were not. Customs duties could be paid by consumers and were collected by the government in the form of a levy on the colonists' income.

The tax on real estate in the colonies was similar to that on personal property. The British Crown owned the lands in the colonies through the "public domain," and property owners were obligated to submit to the control of the Crown. This meant that colonists had limited control over their own land and could not sell it without the approval of the British government. The purpose of this was to reduce the number of colonists living on their land and to maintain British control over the colonies.

The British government used taxes to fund its own expenditures and to pay for the government's own operations. The colonies also imposed their own taxes and levied tariffs or duties to fund their own government expenditures. Taxation was a fundamental part of British economic policy, and many historians have called it "the oldest and most enduring feature of [the British] financial system."

Because the colonists controlled their own wealth and property, taxes were a key way for the British government to maintain control over the colonies. The colonists created their own local systems of taxation to protect their own interests and privileges, such as tariffs on goods carried by settlers. Taxes helped merchants compete with foreign traders and maintain their control of the British market.

The colonists had very few rights against the British government, as taxes were collected primarily by the Crown and often, the British government refused to collect taxes unless the colonists paid up or the revenue was used for services for the colonies. The British Parliament claimed that the colonists had no right to resist taxation, and that they were obligated to pay taxes to the British government.

The American College of Cardiology (ACC) has recently released the findings of a massive global study investigating the impact of exercise on the heart, specifically in individuals with heart failure (HF). HF occurs when the heart is unable to pump blood effectively due to atherosclerotic plaques narrowing the aorta.

According to the ACC, exercise has been shown to reduce the incidence of HF by a significant 8% in individuals at risk. The study, which spanned over 5.3 years and involved over 300,000 participants from 28 countries, suggests that regular physical activity can make a substantial difference in heart health.

Dr. Michael T. Moritz, Chair of the ACC's Cardiology Section and lead author of the study, emphasizes that exercise is not a one-size-fits-all solution. While the study demonstrates the benefits of regular exercise, it's essential to tailor exercise programs to individual needs and health status. Dr. Moritz also notes that the study did not investigate the effects of increased exercise duration on cardiovascular disease and HF, but he believes that further research will provide more insight into this area.

Interestingly, a previous study in the Netherlands reported modest benefits from high-intensity exercise (HIIT) on cardiovascular disease. However, this trial was suspended due to serious complications, including sudden death and cardiovascular arrest.

Despite these findings, there is now a growing body of evidence indicating that regular aerobic exercise can improve heart failure outcomes. The ACC will continue to conduct research to determine the benefits of improving fitness among individuals with heart failure.

It's essential to note that these studies were conducted on diverse age groups and disease populations, making it difficult to generalize the findings to specific individuals. However, they do suggest a strong link between regular exercise and heart failure, and may help demystify the condition for those who have already been treated for heart failure or other heart-related conditions.

In the short term, exercise appears to be a valuable tool for managing cardiovascular disease and heart failure. If you're one of these individuals, it's crucial to take advantage of available treatments, including exercise, under the guidance of a healthcare professional.

The US Supreme Court has struck down Ohio's restrictive marriage laws, ruling 5-4 in favor of same-sex couples. This landmark decision, Obergefell v. Hodges, has been years in the making, and it's a major victory for the LGBTQ+ community.

I caught up with Tim Dickinson, a former staff writer for The Times and now a managing editor at NPR member station WNPR, to get his take on the ruling. "It's a big shock to Washington, D.C.," he said, echoing the sentiments of many in the nation's capital.

So, what does this mean for same-sex couples in Ohio and beyond? The majority opinion doesn't actually overturn marriage laws, but rather makes it unconstitutional to deny any legal recognition to same-sex couples. This means that same-sex couples in Ohio will finally be able to get married, and it's likely to have a ripple effect across the country.

But what about states that want to ban same-sex marriage? According to Tim, these states will have to give up some control over marriage laws and allow same-sex couples to marry. It's a major shift, and one that's likely to have far-reaching implications.

As for DOMA, the Defense of Marriage Act, it's likely to be struck down in the near future. The Supreme Court has already hinted that it's unconstitutional, and this ruling could be the final nail in the coffin.

Overall, this is a major victory for the LGBTQ+ community, and a step towards greater equality and justice for all.

Before we dive into the recipe, make sure all your ingredients are at room temperature, nice and cozy. Preheat your oven to a toasty 325 degrees Fahrenheit. Now, let's get started with the cake batter. In a bowl, whisk together a cup of flour until it's smooth and lovely. Gradually add in some sugar, and mix until just combined. Don't overdo it, just get it mixed up nicely.

Next, knead the batter for about 10 rounds - it's like giving it a little massage! Place a spoonful of baking soda on top, and let it sit for a bit until the surface reaches about a teaspoon in diameter. Scoop out small amounts of the batter using an ice cream scoop, and place them in a large baking pan. You'll be building a little mountain!

Now, heat the batter over low heat in a bowl for about 10 minutes, then pop it in the oven. While that's baking, let's make the topping. In a separate bowl, use a wooden spoon to break up some baking soda into teeny-tiny balls. Add some powdered sugar, and mix until it's all combined and lovely.

Sprinkle a bit more baking powder on top of the cake, and pop it back in the oven for 30-45 minutes. And that's it! You'll have a delicious cake to enjoy.

Hardy's study, published in the Journal of the American Veterinary Association, suggests that dogs are surprisingly sensitive to questions about identity and belonging. When asked if they were the "right" dog, the dogs in the bathroom stall became nearly twice as uncomfortable as those in the room with their owners. It's as if they just want to be told if they're in the right place or not.

While Hardy didn't explicitly address the implications of her findings, she did hint that the results might be different if the questions were asked in a bedroom instead of a bathroom. And let's be real, who hasn't wondered what their dog is thinking when they're alone in the bathroom?

The concept of the commons has become a powerful tool for social movements, as it allows for the creation and sharing of resources in a way that promotes mutual interdependence and social solidarity. In this sense, the commons is the very fabric of society, and it's what defines our relationships with one another and the resources we rely on.

But what exactly is the commons? It's the space where social users come together to create, consume, and share goods and services. It's inclusive by nature, encompassing everyone regardless of social class. The commons is the antithesis of state or corporate ownership, where resources are controlled for personal gain or exclusive use.

In a commons society, resources are shared among all users, and everyone has a stake in maintaining the system. This is in contrast to exclusive social relations, where ownership is limited to a select few. Exclusive relations can take many forms, from private relationships to public or economic ones. In each case, access is restricted, and those who don't fit the criteria are excluded.

But what about commoning activities? Let's take the example of New Orleans' "crowd-sourced water" initiative. The city created a shared social space, the "Boulevard of the Crescent City," where residents can access water tokens, or "Water Cents," at various locations along the boulevard. This innovative approach allows for efficient use of resources, as the water can be distributed to multiple locations and users can share the tokens. The result is a more equitable and sustainable system, where everyone has access to the resources they need.

This kind of shared social space is what the commons is all about. It's a space where people come together to create, share, and maintain resources, promoting social solidarity and mutual interdependence. By embracing the commons, we can build a more just and equitable society, where everyone has access to the resources they need to thrive.

In a significant blow to Massachusetts' gun control efforts, a federal appeals court has struck down a law requiring certain employers, including retail giant Wal-Mart, to post signs detailing their gun policies. The American Civil Liberties Union of Massachusetts and the Center for American Progress, a liberal think tank, had challenged the law, arguing it violated First Amendment protections of free speech.

Wal-Mart, which had initially supported the law, later flipped and argued that the requirement to post its gun policy on its website would not only infringe on its First Amendment rights but also hinder its ability to protect its property. The company claimed that the law would impose significant burdens on both itself and its store managers, causing many workers to refrain from expressing their support for the company.

In its argument, Wal-Mart pointed out that the law would effectively ban employees from displaying a broad majority of its views on its website, forcing the company to adopt a policy that prohibits political and other expressions. This, in turn, would drive away some workers.

The court's ruling is notable, as it marks the second time a federal court has struck down a gun law that restricts employees' free speech rights. In 2008, the court ruled that federal law trumps state law on gun control, and in this case, it has gone beyond that ruling, striking down a law that requires employers to post their gun policies.

The decision is significant, as it sets a precedent for employers' rights to free speech and the limits of government regulation. The Supreme Court has previously upheld limits on companies' ability to punish employees who exercise their right to express themselves, and this ruling further solidifies that principle.

Get ready to cozy up with a warm and comforting bowl of sweet potato soup! First, preheat your oven to a toasty 350°F (175°C). While that's heating up, take 2 big sweet potatoes and peel them into 1/4 inch cubes. Spread them out on a baking sheet, drizzle with 1 tablespoon of olive oil, and pop them in the oven for 25-30 minutes, or until they're tender enough to fork into.

Once your sweet potatoes are done, it's time to start cooking the soup. In a large pot, melt 2 tablespoons of butter or olive oil over medium-high heat. Add 1/2 cup of diced onion and sauté until it's soft and fragrant, about 5 minutes.

Now it's time to bring all the ingredients together! Add the cooked sweet potatoes, 4 cups of veggie broth, and 2 tablespoons of grated fresh ginger to the pot. Bring it to a boil, then reduce the heat and let it simmer for about 20 minutes, or until all the veggies are cooked through.

Once the soup is ready, remove it from the heat and blend it until it's smooth and creamy. Finally, pour it into bowls and top it with some chopped fresh herbs, a dollop of plain Greek yogurt, or a splash of hot sauce. Grab a spoon and get cozy – this sweet potato soup is the perfect way to warm up on a chilly day!

Have you ever felt like the stuff that goes into your body - blood, spit, semen, poop, or breast milk - is somehow stuck inside you and might never come back out? Yeah, it's a weird sensation, but scientists are actually studying this phenomenon. They're calling it "extrinsic" factors, and they're finding that things like stress, love, and cravings can send messages from your circulatory system back to your brain. And sometimes, these messages can be super harmful, leading to depression and even suicidal thoughts.

Lead researcher Dr. Charles Raison says that if you're not living a balanced and fulfilling life, the messages that could make you feel good might not be so great in the long run. He's calling for more rigorous studies on these extrinsic factors, because right now, doctors are mostly relying on internal factors like diet and blood pressure.

The study involved 19 patients with depression, all of whom had tried to commit suicide at least once. The researchers checked their blood and urine for changes after their symptoms appeared. They found that the patients' diets were all over the place, with some eating a lot of protein and others eating hardly any. But the blood samples showed that these changes weren't the only factors at play.

Dr. Raison says that doctors can try to adjust patients' diets and hormones through pills, shots, and other treatments, but it's no guarantee. Some evidence even suggests that these adjustments might not do much to prevent worsening moods or suicide attempts.

So, what's the takeaway? We still don't know what kind of diet is best for people with depression, and we need more research to figure it out. But Dr. Raison is optimistic that by investigating all the messages our bodies send to our brains, we can find a way to help people feel better and live healthier lives.

The humble electric shower head - a game-changer for large families or those who are always on-the-go. But with so many options out there, it can be tough to know which one is right for you. That's why we're diving into the world of electric showers, exploring the differences between direct current (DC) and alternating current (AC) electric shower heads.

DC electric shower heads are perfect for older homes with older water heaters and electrical controls. They're not the most efficient, but they get the job done. These shower heads typically have a smaller diameter and require more water to function properly. You'll need a bucket or tub to collect the water, plus an outlet and faucet to connect to.

On the other hand, AC electric shower heads are ideal for new and existing properties. They're bigger, more efficient, and perfect for large homes and multi-family dwellings. This is a landmark ruling, as it's the first time a high court has addressed the issue of the right to vote for all citizens who haven't registered.

The court has directed the state Election Commission to issue guidelines for handling applications involving Kapoor, who's set to star in the upcoming film "Kabhi Kabhie Gham". The order stipulates that Kapoor's name shouldn't be added to the voter's roll in Maharashtra unless he sends a letter to the state Election Commission. If he doesn't, he'll be considered a non-resident actor.

Kapoor had sued the Maharashtra government, claiming his name shouldn't be added to the voters' list. The court ruled that Kapoor's name would be added to the list if he files an application with the central Election Commission at least twice in one year. He's also free to contest polls at any time.

The court also ordered the Centre to send a list of people allowed to vote with a name other than Kapoor's to the High Court. Kapoor and his lawyer, B B Jain, who filed the PIL, told TOI that the Act allows non-residents like Kapoor to contest in elections, and their petition still stands.

The concept of micro-fertilization has been floating around since the 1980s, and it's all about separating immature sperm from the healthy stuff. The goal is to create a process that allows for the creation, use, and removal of embryos without relying on human embryo donation. Essentially, scientists want to develop a technique that can mix and match sperm without the need for a human embryo.

Initially, it was thought that this process could only work if the sperm contained mitochondria, aka "solar cells." But, a team of scientists at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem has made a breakthrough, demonstrating the existence of micro-fertilization and testing it in Israel and the US. The process involves separating immature sperm from healthy sperm, and in some cases, transferring the maternal DNA to create a hybrid.

Now, here's the thing - there's no indication that this process has been tested on human embryos yet. However, studies have shown that it can work on human sperm that are fertilized in vitro, without the need for embryo donation.

So, what does this mean for infertility patients? It could be a game-changer if it's true. But, let's be real - it's still theoretical. This method might allow a woman to conceive a healthy child with no inherited diseases and a normal life. But, it would require the parents to provide the maternal DNA, which would essentially mean using an embryo donation process. In that case, micro-fertilization could help women avoid the risks associated with IVF.

Some researchers are exploring the potential of micro-fertilization for kids with genetic disorders caused by gene mutations. The Hebrew University is actually conducting a study on how this technique might impact children with genetic disorders carried by older parents.

So, what do you think about micro-fertilization? Are the potential benefits worth the potential drawbacks?

The United States is drowning in antibiotics, and the world is following suit. According to the FDA's own data, our reliance on over-the-counter medications and supplements like antibiotics and probiotics is fueling a superbug epidemic. The United Nations and Brazil are taking steps to address the issue, but it's a tough fight. A group of scientists has launched a campaign called "Be Bold. Don't Use Antibiotics" to push the FDA to take action.

A recent study published in PLOS Biology highlights the alarming rise of multidrug-resistant organisms, which are linked to serious and often fatal infections. The study has garnered significant media attention, but the question on everyone's mind is: why are Americans consuming such massive quantities of antibiotics? The answer lies in our country's war on the environment.

The CDC reports that 2.1 billion prescriptions are written annually for antibiotics, resulting in 10,000 deaths daily due to antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Dr. Paul M. Offit, a professor at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, bluntly states, "We're doing something wrong, even if it's unintentional." He believes that changing the way we use antibiotics on farms could solve the problem.

Antibiotics are meant to be a last resort to combat bacterial infections. However, they only work against some bacteria, not all. Over time, the drugs can destroy a bacteria's ability to survive, leading to the development of "super-resistant bacteria" that can be as deadly as cancer. The CDC estimates that if you're given 30 billion antibiotics, your chance of survival is a mere 1%.

The problem is compounded by the fact that antibiotics don't work against all bacteria. As a result, superbugs are emerging at an alarming rate. The CDC predicts that by 2050, 75% of the world's bacteria may be resistant to drugs, leaving one in four people infected with a resistant bacterium without a treatment option.

A recent study published in July found that bacteria have mutated to become immune to some, but not all, antibiotics. The FDA is aware of the issue and has been working to address it, but the scientific community is calling for more action. It's time for us to take a step back and re-examine our reliance on antibiotics.

The CIA's Secret Spy Tool: A Tale of Mysterious Code and Hidden Intentions

But some documents were missing, and the inspector general's team was left in the dark. They demanded answers, and eventually, the CIA provided a document describing a spyware program called CIAGRU. The team was furious, and the Justice Department and FBI were also outraged.

The CIA claimed to have no record of the spyware program, but later produced another document describing it as CIAGRU 2.0. This raised even more red flags, as it was linked to a classified intelligence document. The case against Hinckley continued, with a federal judge eventually dismissing all charges.

The ancient rivalry between Taoism and Confucianism lies in their fundamentally different approaches to understanding the world. While Taoism clings to traditional philosophies, Confucianism champions modern principles. This dichotomy is reflected in the societies they envision. Taoism sees a harmonious balance between individual and collective, with each contributing to the greater good. Confucianism, on the other hand, is built around the concept of a unified state, where individuals submit to a higher authority.

Mao Tsi-tung, the enigmatic leader of China's communist revolution, once astutely observed that the core difference between these two philosophies lies in their understanding of society. In ancient China, society was a collection of individuals who contributed their unique perspectives to create a rich tapestry of thought. Later, this dynamic shifted, and society became a collective of individuals who contributed their energies to create a new, unified whole. This fundamental concept remains at the heart of Chinese society today, with its intricate web of relationships and competing ideologies.

A coalition of prominent civil rights organizations has launched a fierce campaign to dismantle North Carolina's recently passed "bathroom bill," House Bill 2 (HB2). The American Civil Liberties Union, National Organization for Women, National Disability Rights Network, and Campaign for Black Lives, among others, are calling on state lawmakers to repeal the measure in the next legislative session and urging the US Justice Department to investigate the law's constitutionality.

The groups are adamant that HB2 is a step backward, reviving the discriminatory practices of the Jim Crow era. "HB2 is an attack on civil rights and equality," said Catherine Lhamon, executive director of the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund. "It's a return to a time when people were judged based on their race and gender, rather than their character and abilities."

The groups are also warning that HB2 will have far-reaching consequences, allowing businesses to discriminate against transgender individuals and creating a culture of fear and intolerance. "HB2 is not just about transgender people," said Lhamon. "It's about all individuals who don't conform to gender stereotypes. It's about women and girls being forced to use bathrooms that don't feel safe or welcoming to them."

The groups are also criticizing the law's provision allowing individuals to use facilities that correspond with their assigned birth sex, without proper identification. This, they argue, creates a loophole for individuals to engage in inappropriate behavior without consequence.

In response to the criticism, proponents of HB2 argue that the law is necessary to protect the privacy and safety of individuals who don't identify with their biological sex. However, opponents argue that the law is based on unfounded fears and stereotypes, and that it will only serve to further marginalize and discriminate against already vulnerable communities.

As the debate rages on, the ACLU and other groups are vowing to hold lawmakers accountable for their actions, including Governor Pat McCrory, who has used federal taxpayer dollars to defend the legislation. "It's time for lawmakers who have defended discriminatory laws to be held to account, no matter where they run," said Lhamon.

A team of astronomers has made a groundbreaking discovery using NASA's Hubble Space Telescope and the Keck II telescope in Hawaii. The team's findings are significant because they provide evidence for the existence of a type of white dwarf star that has been predicted but never directly observed. The supernova, known as SN 1987A, is one of the most distant ever recorded and was seen in 1988. The researchers used Hubble images to search for evidence of a supernova and found a surprising alignment between the supernova and the plane of the galaxy.

The team hypothesized that the white dwarf found in SN 1987A could be the parent of SN 1997A2, and they used Hubble images to test this idea. They found that SN 1987A1 was more spread out, indicating that the white dwarf was closer to the disk of its host galaxy. As the white dwarf grew brighter, the galaxies it was orbiting started crossing in front of it, creating a more dense, hot disc.

The researchers also found that SN 1987A1 was more likely to be a result of a merger of white dwarfs, rather than a single white dwarf becoming unstable. This theory fits well with the data from SN 1987A1 and provides a simple explanation for the supernova's properties.

The team plans to analyze more detailed images of SN 1987A2 from other telescopes and determine whether or not it is actually a supernova. They will look for the signal that they predicted it should have, and if they can identify it, they will know that they have found a new type of supernova.
